place.zh: 沂中医 · 一食堂后门 · 夜

setup.zh: 食堂后门的垃圾站，一条叫人踢过的土狗。他蹲下，吸四吐六，等它自己过来。十一月二日早上，雷老师的指头，马氏大药房的箱子，菜单上的泡面碗印。
setup.en: The bins behind the canteen, a stray that has been kicked. He crouches, in four, out six, and waits for it to come. The morning of November the second: Coach Lei's fingers, the box from Ma's Pharmacy, a noodle-bowl ring on the menu.

recap.zh: 吸四吐六收服了红薯；雷老师「……接着投」；补剂箱里的龙马强力胶囊，一粒一杯美式，「一真，一半，一假」；菜单上的泡面碗印，「下回说实话」。
recap.en: In four, out six, and Sweet Potato came to him; Coach Lei's "...Keep shooting"; the Dragon-Horse capsules in the supplement box, an americano apiece, "one real, one half, one fake"; the noodle-bowl ring on the menu, "tell the truth next time".

zh: 半块烤红薯，搁在手心里。
en: Half a roast sweet potato on his open palm.
"Dogs don't join the team." "How many beats?"

story.zh:
那天晚饭他没去食堂。年级群里已经有了那段视频，配的字是「论一个罚球可以离篮筐多远」；表白墙上有人发帖：「0号是谁？能不能把他送去院系杯，我们学院想抽到针推。」六点多，他妈发来一条六十秒的语音，头一句：「芒啊，家长群里那个投篮的，又是你吧？」第二句是他爸，离手机远，嗓门大：「罚球我知道，就是站着投，没人拦你。站着都投不进，下回你坐着投。」后头五十秒，是他妈在骂他爸。

他把手机扣在桌上。对床的眼镜从一本图书馆的《庄子》后头抬起头，指头点着一行：「『[缘督以为经]{典=zhuangzi-yangshengzhu}』。督，是脊梁正中那一道。你那第二个，背都弓了。」

「那刹车那一路呢？」沈芒道，「阿禾说，吐气是踩刹车。解剖课上那两根白线——」

眼镜想了想：「迷走神经从脖子两边下来，管心、管肺、管肚子，走的是身子前头。你要非给它找个座位，就坐任脉那一路，前头正中那一道。」他扶了扶眼镜，「这是比附。医书上没这么写，你别拿去考试。」

上铺的老蔡一拍床板：「懂了！背挺直，是督；长吐一口，是任——练气入门，先通任督二脉！」眼镜一口气噎在嗓子眼，脸都憋红了，张嘴要骂，想了想，没骂。

九点多他饿得顶不住，又不想端着餐盘从一千多双眼睛前头走过去，绕到了一食堂后门。后门是垃圾站，一排绿色的大桶，桶边一盏昏黄的灯，门口一个推车卖烤红薯的老头收摊收了一半。他花三块钱买了最后一个。老头一边往炉子里捅火钩子，一边朝垃圾桶那头努努嘴：「留神那个小东西。暑假里不知道谁扔这儿的，叫人踢过，谁都不让靠。前两天两个学生拿火腿肠逗它，伸着手往前凑，差一点叫它咬了。」说罢推着车走了。

垃圾桶后头，「呜」的一声。

灯影里一条土狗，不大，红黄的毛脏成一绺一绺，脑门正中一撮毛直直地立着，像长了一只角。它压低身子，耳朵往后贴，喉咙里呜呜地响，一双眼睛死死盯着他手里的红薯，又盯着他的脸。

沈芒小时候在德州乡下，叫邻居家的大黄狗追过三条街，裤子后头撕了一个口子，那个口子他妈补了，他到今天还记得。两条腿先软了，心跳一下子蹿上来，比下午站在罚球线上还快。那狗也在怕：往后缩，背上的毛一根一根竖起来，尾巴夹在两条后腿中间，喉咙里的声音越来越凶。

他先试了那两个学生的法子：站直了，把红薯往前一伸，嘴里「来来来」地哄。那狗往后一缩，猛地往前一蹿，「啪」，牙在他指头前半尺合上了。他往后一跳，跳得比这辈子哪一回起跳都高，红薯差点脱手。他妈从小念叨：叫狗抓破一点皮，就得去打狂犬疫苗，一针不能少。方才那一口再近半尺，他今晚就得在校医院排队。那狗退回桶后头，背上的毛炸得更高，喉咙里的声音又凶了一倍。

一个怕，一个更怕；一个越怕越凶，一个越凶越怕。他忽然觉得这场面他见过——下午，罚球线上，他也是越怕越憋，越憋越抖。沈芒啊沈芒，你在罚球线上怕一圈人，在这儿怕一条狗，你这一天，怕了个全套。

吐气。

他慢慢侧过身子，蹲下来，眼睛看地。吸，四拍。吐，六拍——吐得长长的，像把一整天的气都从身子里放出去。一口，两口，三口。心口那阵乱跳慢了下来；那狗喉咙里的声音，也停了。

他把红薯掰成两半，大的那一半搁在摊开的手心里，手背贴地，不往前送，就那么蹲着，等。那狗的鼻子先动，眼睛却钉在他脸上，钉了足有半分钟，才一步一步挪过来，伸长了脖子，从他手心里叼走那半块红薯，退回灯底下吃了起来，吃两口，抬眼看他一下。

他蹲着没动，攥着自己那半块红薯的手在膝盖上一下一下地抖——不是怕的抖了，是乐的。他在心里小小声地喊了一句：

成了！

那狗吃完了，连地上的渣都舔干净了，犹豫了一会儿，慢吞吞走近两步，嗅了嗅他的拖鞋，在离他一步远的地方趴了下来，下巴搁在前爪上，眼睛半睁半闭，还瞄着他。它脖子上挂着一个绿塑料牌子，他借着灯光凑过去看：「沂中医动保社　已绝育　已免疫」。他松了一口气——方才光顾着乐，压根没想到这一层。

「你叫什么？」狗没理他。「那就叫红薯吧。你吃了我半个红薯，你就叫红薯。」他单手摸出手机，拍了一张照片：昏黄的灯，一只拖鞋，一步开外一颗毛茸茸的脑袋。发给阿禾。

「狗不进队。」隔了一会儿，「几拍？」

「吸四，吐六。五口。」

「记了。」

垃圾站的灯底下，一个人蹲着，一条狗趴着，没有一个人看着。没人看着的时候，他行。可是十一月七号，看台上会有一千双眼睛。红薯翻了个身，换了一边脸，眼睛到底闭上了。他的腿早蹲麻了，麻得像别人的，也没敢动。食堂后厨还亮着灯，里头有人在刷锅，水声哗哗的。

十一月二日早上六点，他一个人在罚球线上吸四吐六。雷老师进门：「罚球前深吸一口，憋住，手才稳。我带了二十年队。」

他把雷老师两根指头按在雷老师自己的腕子上：「您吸四拍……吐六拍。」

吐到一半，雷老师的眉毛动了一下，把手背到了身后：「……接着投。」

球馆另一头，咯吱，咯吱，咯吱。马小宝在摇他的大摇杯，一升的杯子，里头一颗不锈钢的弹簧球，撞得杯壁咯吱咯吱响，像一只吃不饱的老鼠在磨牙。他摇三十下，拧开盖子一仰脖灌半杯，又倒两勺粉，接着摇。「一天四杯。早上一杯，练完一杯，下午一杯，睡前一杯。」他咂了咂嘴，「喝完了，还饿。」

六点二十，雷老师抱着一只大纸箱进来，往中圈一撂，侧面四个红字：马氏大药房。「赞助的，这个月的。自己分。」一群人围上去拆箱子像拆年货。头一样乳清蛋白粉，桶大得能当凳子坐；第二样一罐白粉末，「一水肌酸」；第三样压在最底下，一摞金灿灿的小盒子，盒面上一匹红马驮着一只大鹿角，六个烫金大字：**龙马强力胶囊**，底下一行小字：「千年古方 · 人参鹿茸精华 · 增肌三倍」。蛋白粉和肌酸叫几个老队员分了；那一摞龙马，老队员看都不看，叫几个新来的抢了个精光。沈芒手慢，没抢着。

马小宝抄起一盒，扔进他怀里：「拿着。队友价，零元。三倍。下回我犯你，你好歹有劲把球扔到筐上。」

沈芒捧着那只金盒子，像捧着一块刚出炉的金砖。增肌三倍。试训那天第五个推不起来，叫马小宝把杠接了去；阿禾本子上他那一行力量，至今是红的。他把盒子翻过来看了又看，心跳都快了。

「你一回吃几粒？」

「我一粒都不吃。」马小宝摇着摇杯，「那是卖给外人的。我爸说的。」

「那你吃的什么？」

马小宝把摇杯在手心里掂了一掂，没回头：「国外的。NBA都用。」咯吱咯吱，走了。

阿禾的笔尖在本子上停了一下。她从他手里拿过盒子翻到背面，指着那行比蚂蚁还小的字：「人参提取物。鹿茸粉。咖啡因，每粒一百毫克——一粒，一杯美式。咖啡因是真东西，能让人一时觉得有劲、不困；可它是借的，借完了要还。借来的油门，不长肉。」她拿笔尖往箱子那边一指，「一箱三样：蛋白粉是吃的，不是药，奶里提出来的，跟鸡蛋一个道理；肌酸有点用；这个，」笔尖敲了敲金盒子，「一真，一半，一假。」

眼镜在场边举着手机：「我查了。《本草》人参那一条，『[久服，轻身、延年。]{典=shennong-renshen}』——一个字没讲长肉。」

阿禾伸手到他书包里一抽，带出一张叠着的 A4 纸，昨天她在食堂门口给的「沈芒 · 菜单（两周）」，纸上一圈油印子，正好一个碗口大，洇在「米饭」两个字上。

「泡面碗。」她道，「十月里我问你吃什么，你说食堂。」

沈芒的脸烧了起来。他最怕的就是这一刻：她那本子上，他这一行底下，添上那三个字。

阿禾的笔没落下去。她把纸叠好塞回去：「下回说实话。没钱，菜单可以改。」

那天夜里，沈芒把金盒子塞进书包最底下，拉上了拉链。那张洇了油的菜单，他铺平了，头一行：「早饭：鸡蛋两个。」

十点，视频没来，来的是电话。他妈的声音压得很低，背景里有人喊号：「你爸在服务区下车，腿一软，跪下了。起不来。」医院的片子他妈念不全，念到「半月板」三个字卡住了。「大夫说，起码歇三个月。车，车队先收回去了。」顿了一顿，又道：「你那集训，还要交钱不？」

「……不用交钱，队里管饭。」

电话那头换了人，是他爸，疼得直抽气，还要补刀：「没事儿，跪着也是站着，矮一截。」话没说完，又「嘶」了一声。

沈芒攥着手机，嘴比脑子快：「爸，你先别往里吸气，往外吐，吐得长一点，比吸的长。」那头没声了，只有一口很长、很抖的气，从手机里一点一点漏出来。过了好一会儿，他爸道：「……还真松一点。」

挂了电话，他把《针灸学》翻到膝盖那一页，抄下「犊鼻」「足三里」，抄完了，又翻到底下一行小字：半月板撕裂，针灸只能止痛，撕开的地方，多半长不回来。他盯着「长不回来」四个字看了很久，把书合上了。家里一个月的进项，眼下只剩他妈超市那一份；他办健身卡花掉的那两百块车票钱，忽然就不是车票钱了。

离院系杯头一轮，五天。
story.en:
He skipped dinner at the canteen that evening. The video was already in the year group, captioned "On how far a free throw can be from the basket"; on the confessions wall someone had posted: "Who is Number 0? Can we send him to the College Cup? Our college wants to draw Acupuncture." After six, his mom sent a sixty-second voice message. The first sentence: "Mang, the one shooting baskets in the parents' group — that's you again, isn't it?" The second was his dad, far from the phone, loud: "Free throws, I know those — you just stand there and shoot, nobody's stopping you. If you can't make it standing, next time shoot sitting down." The last fifty seconds were his mom telling his dad off.

He put the phone face down on the desk. Specs, on the opposite bed, looked up from behind a library *Zhuangzi* and tapped a line with his finger: "'Follow the du as your constant.' The du is the line right down the middle of the spine. On that second one, your back was hunched."

"And the brake line?" said Shen Mang. "Ahe says breathing out is the brake. Those two white threads in anatomy —"

Specs thought about it: "The vagus nerve comes down both sides of the neck and runs the heart, the lungs, the belly — it travels the front of the body. If you insist on giving it a seat, it sits on the ren channel, the line down the middle of the front." He pushed up his glasses. "That's an analogy. The medical books don't say it. Don't take it into an exam."

Old Cai slapped the bed board up top: "Got it! Back straight, that's the du; one long breath out, that's the ren — first step in qi training, open the Ren and Du channels!" Specs choked on his own breath, went red in the face, opened his mouth to tell him off, thought about it, and didn't.

After nine, too hungry to hold out and unwilling to carry a tray past a thousand pairs of eyes, he went round to the back door of Canteen One. The back was the rubbish station: a row of big green bins, a dim yellow lamp beside them, and at the gate an old man with a roast-sweet-potato cart, half packed up. He paid three yuan for the last one. The old man, poking the fire with his hook, jerked his chin at the bins: "Watch out for that little thing. Someone dumped it here over the summer; it's been kicked, won't let anyone near. Couple of days ago two students tried to coax it with a ham sausage, leaning in with their hands out — nearly got bitten." With that he wheeled his cart away.

From behind the bins, a low "wuu".

In the shadow of the lamp was a mongrel, not big, its reddish-yellow coat matted into dirty clumps, a tuft of hair standing straight up in the middle of its forehead like a single horn. It crouched low, ears flat back, a growl in its throat, eyes fixed hard on the sweet potato in his hand, then on his face.

As a boy in the Dezhou countryside Shen Mang had been chased three streets by the neighbours' big yellow dog; it had torn the seat of his trousers, his mom had patched it, and he remembered it to this day. His legs went soft first, and his heart leapt up faster than it had on the free-throw line that afternoon. The dog was afraid too: it backed off, the hair rose along its spine one strand at a time, its tail went between its hind legs, and the sound in its throat grew fiercer.

He tried the two students' method first: stood up straight, held the sweet potato out, and coaxed, "Here, here, here." The dog shrank back, then lunged; snap — its teeth closed half a foot from his fingers. He jumped back, higher than he had ever jumped in his life, and nearly dropped the sweet potato. His mom had drilled it into him since he was small: one scratch from a dog and it's rabies shots, not one jab fewer. Half a foot closer, and he'd have spent tonight queuing at the campus clinic. The dog retreated behind the bins, the hair on its back bristling higher, the sound in its throat twice as fierce.

One was afraid, the other more afraid; the one got fiercer the more afraid it was, the other more afraid the fiercer it got. He suddenly felt he'd seen this scene before — that afternoon, on the free-throw line, the more afraid he was the harder he'd held his breath, and the harder he held it the more he shook. Shen Mang, oh Shen Mang: afraid of a ring of people on the line, afraid of a dog back here — today you've been afraid of the full set.

Breathe out.

Slowly he turned side-on, squatted, eyes on the ground. In, four counts. Out, six counts — long, as if letting the whole day's air out of his body. One breath, two, three. The wild thumping in his chest slowed down; the sound in the dog's throat stopped too.

He broke the sweet potato in two and set the bigger half in his open palm, back of the hand on the ground, not pushing it forward, just squatting there, waiting. The dog's nose moved first, but its eyes stayed nailed to his face a good half minute before it inched over, step by step, stretched out its neck, took the half sweet potato from his palm, and retreated under the lamp to eat it — two bites, then a glance up at him.

He stayed squatting and didn't move, the hand holding his own half shaking on his knee, over and over — not from fear now, from joy. Inside, very softly, he called out:

Done it!

When the dog had finished, licked up every crumb on the ground, it hesitated, then slowly came two steps nearer, sniffed his slipper, and lay down one pace away, chin on its forepaws, eyes half shut, still watching him. Round its neck hung a green plastic tag; he leaned in under the lamp to read it: "Yizhong Animal Welfare Society · Neutered · Vaccinated." He let out a breath — too busy being glad just now, he hadn't thought of that at all.

"What's your name?" The dog ignored him. "Sweet Potato, then. You ate half my sweet potato, so you're Sweet Potato." One-handed he got out his phone and took a picture: the dim lamp, one slipper, a furry head one pace away. He sent it to Ahe.

"Dogs don't make the team." A while later: "How many counts?"

"In for four, out for six. Five breaths."

"Recorded."

Under the rubbish-station lamp, a person squatting, a dog lying down, and no one watching. When no one was watching, he could do it. But on November the seventh there would be a thousand pairs of eyes in the stands. Sweet Potato rolled over, changed cheeks, and its eyes finally closed. His legs had long since gone numb from squatting, numb as somebody else's, and he still didn't dare move. The canteen kitchen was still lit; inside, someone was scrubbing pots, the water splashing.

At six in the morning on November the second, he was alone at the free-throw line, in for four, out for six. Coach Lei came in: "Before a free throw, take a deep breath and hold it, that's what steadies your hand. I've coached twenty years."

He pressed two of Coach Lei's fingers onto Coach Lei's own wrist: "You breathe in four counts... out six counts."

Halfway through the breath out, Coach Lei's eyebrows twitched, and he put his hands behind his back: "...Keep shooting."

From the other end of the gym: squeak, squeak, squeak. Ma Xiaobao was shaking his big shaker — a one-litre cup with a steel spring ball inside that rattled against the walls like a hungry rat gnawing. He shook it thirty times, unscrewed the lid, tipped his head back and downed half, poured in two more scoops of powder, and shook again. "Four a day. One in the morning, one after training, one in the afternoon, one before bed." He smacked his lips. "Finish it, and I'm still hungry."

At six-twenty Coach Lei came in hugging a big cardboard box and dumped it in the centre circle, four red characters on the side: Ma's Pharmacy. "Sponsor's. This month's. Divide it up yourselves." A crowd closed in and tore into it like New Year parcels. First, whey protein, in a tub big enough to sit on; second, a jar of white powder, "creatine monohydrate"; third, at the very bottom, a stack of small gold boxes, a red horse on the lid carrying a great pair of antlers, six characters stamped in gilt: Dragon-Horse Power Capsules, and a line of small print beneath: "Thousand-year formula · Ginseng & Deer Antler Essence · Triple Muscle Gain." The protein and the creatine were divided among a few of the old hands; the stack of Dragon-Horse the old hands didn't so much as glance at, and the newcomers snatched them clean. Shen Mang was slow, and got none.

Ma Xiaobao scooped up a box and tossed it into his arms: "Take it. Teammate price, zero yuan. Triple. Next time I foul you, at least you'll have the strength to get the ball to the rim."

Shen Mang held the gold box like a gold brick fresh from the kiln. Triple muscle gain. At tryouts the fifth rep hadn't gone up and Ma Xiaobao had taken the bar off him; the strength entry on his line in Ahe's notebook was still in red. He turned the box over and over, and his heart beat faster.

"How many do you take at a time?"

"I don't take a single one." Ma Xiaobao shook his shaker. "Those are for selling to outsiders. My dad said so."

"Then what do you take?"

Ma Xiaobao weighed the shaker in his palm and didn't look back: "Imported. The NBA uses it." Squeak, squeak, and he was gone.

Ahe's pen tip paused on the notebook. She took the box from his hands, turned it over, and pointed to a line of print smaller than ants: "Ginseng extract. Deer antler powder. Caffeine, a hundred milligrams a capsule — one capsule, one americano. Caffeine is real; it makes you feel strong and awake for a while. But it's borrowed, and borrowed has to be paid back. A borrowed accelerator. Builds no muscle." Her pen tip pointed at the box. "Three things in one carton: protein powder is food, not medicine — it's from milk, same idea as an egg; creatine is some use; and this," the pen tip tapped the gold box, "one real, one half, one fake."

Specs, at the sideline, held up his phone: "I looked it up. In the *Bencao*, the entry on ginseng: 'Taken long, it lightens the body and lengthens the years.' — Not one word about building muscle."

Ahe reached into his backpack and pulled out a folded sheet of A4 — the "Shen Mang · Menu (Two Weeks)" she had given him at the canteen door yesterday. On it was a ring of grease, exactly the size of a bowl's rim, soaked into the word "rice."

"Instant-noodle bowl," she said. "In October I asked what you ate, and you said the canteen."

Shen Mang's face burned. This was the moment he had dreaded most: those three words going in under his line in her notebook.

Ahe's pen didn't come down. She folded the sheet and slid it back: "Tell the truth next time. No money — the menu can be changed."

That night Shen Mang stuffed the gold box into the very bottom of his backpack and zipped it shut. The grease-stained menu he smoothed out flat; the first line: "Breakfast: two eggs."

At ten it wasn't a video call; it was a phone call. His mother kept her voice low, someone calling numbers behind her: "Your dad got out at a service station and his leg gave way. He went down on his knees. Couldn't get up." She couldn't read the whole scan report out; she got as far as "meniscus" and stuck. "The doctor says three months off at least. The truck — the fleet's taken it back for now." A pause. "That training camp of yours — do you have to pay for it?"

"…No, it's free. The team covers meals."

The phone changed hands. It was his father, sucking air through his teeth with the pain, and still getting a dig in: "No big deal. Kneeling's just standing, a bit shorter." Before he finished there was another hiss.

Shen Mang gripped the phone, his mouth faster than his head: "Dad, don't breathe in yet — breathe out, and make it long, longer than the breath in." The line went quiet; there was only one long, shaking breath leaking out of the phone, bit by bit. After a good while his father said: "…It does ease a bit."

When he hung up he turned his *Acupuncture* textbook to the knee page and copied out "Dubi" and "Zusanli"; then he turned to a line of small print further down: torn meniscus — acupuncture only eases the pain; where it's torn, it mostly won't grow back. He stared at "won't grow back" for a long time and shut the book. The family's money each month was now only his mother's pay from the supermarket; the two hundred yuan of train fare he'd spent on a gym card was suddenly not train fare any more.

Five days to the first round of the College Cup.
